Doping-driven Mott transition from steady-state density functional theory

David Jacob1⋆\star and Stefan Kurth2,3,4

1 Departamento de Física, Universidad de Alicante, Campus de San Vicente del Raspeig, E-03690, Alicante, Spain

2 Nano-Bio Spectroscopy Group and European Theoretical Spectroscopy Facility (ETSF), Departamento de Polímeros y Materiales Avanzados: Física, Química y Tecnología, Universidad del País Vasco EHU, Avenida de Tolosa 72, E-20018 San Sebastián, Spain

3 IKERBASQUE, Basque Foundation for Science, Plaza Euskadi 5, E-48009 Bilbao, Spain

4 Donostia International Physics Center (DIPC), Paseo Manuel de Lardizabal 4, E-20018 San Sebastián, Spain

⋆\star david.jacob@ua.es

Abstract

We describe the doping-driven Mott transition in the Hubbard model within the framework of steady-state density functional theory, or i-DFT. In order to access the many-body spectral function in i-DFT, an approximation to the exchange-correlation (xc) bias at arbitrary density and current is required. By making use of Fermi-liquid theory, we derive conditions on the xc bias of i-DFT in terms of the quasiparticle weight, thus establishing a clear connection between i-DFT and Fermi-liquid theory. The Fermi liquid conditions are then employed to guide the construction of an approximation to the xc bias functional. Numerical results obtained with this functional demonstrate that the doping-driven Mott transition can indeed be captured with i-DFT. More generally, our i-DFT approach to calculate spectral functions establishes an explicit form for the functional relationship between the many-body spectral function and the ground state electronic density.

1 Introduction

A Mott insulator is a material that according to conventional band theory would be classified as a metal [1], but due to strong electronic interactions a gap —the Mott gap— opens in the electronic spectrum, thus turning it into an insulator [2]. The insulating behavior is therefore driven by the interactions between electrons rather than band-filling, as in the case of a normal band insulator. Hence, by tuning the interaction strength a phase transition between a metallic and an insulating phase, known as the Mott (metal-insulator) transition, can be induced [3]. On the other hand, a Mott insulator can also be turned into a metal by doping, e.g., by tuning the chemical potential via a gate or by charge transfer from donor atoms, much like doping of a semiconductor. However, different from semiconductors, which become conducting by fractional occupation of the conduction band, a doped Mott insulator becomes conducting due to the appearance of a quasiparticle band within the Mott gap [4, 5], which owing to the strong electronic interactions is often strongly renormalized [6, 7, 8]. The strong renormalization may give rise to so-called heavy-fermion behavior, where the effective mass of the electrons can be up to a thousand times the free electron mass, leading to peculiar thermodynamic properties of these materials [9]. Ultimately, doped Mott insulators are also thought to be at the heart of high-Tc superconductivity [10].

One of the central models for understanding Mott insulators and strongly correlated materials in general is the Hubbard model [11, 12, 13]. In its simplest version, i.e., the single-band Hubbard model, it consists of a lattice with a single orbital at each lattice site, connected by a hopping tt and a strictly local (on-site) Coulomb repulsion UU. Despite its relative simplicity the Hubbard model not only captures the essence of the Mott metal-insulator transition [14], but gives rise to an extremely rich phase diagram that even includes a superconducting phase [15]. A particularly clear and physically transparent picture of the Mott transition is obtained in the limit of infinite dimensions and the resultant theoretical framework of dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) in terms of local electronic correlations [16, 17, 18]. More recently, the Hubbard model has also been successfully employed for the theoretical description of magnetic nanographenes [19, 20, 21, 22]. Thus, much of research in strongly correlated electrons has traditionally concentrated on the Hubbard model and its ramifications.

While it has always been clear that density functional theory (DFT), being an in principle exact many-body framework, should be capable of describing strongly correlated systems, the application of DFT to strongly correlated materials has been hampered by two serious caveats: (i) the common approximations to the exchange-correlation (xc) functional like LDA and GGA do not properly capture the strong electronic correlations that open the Mott gap, and (ii) the Kohn-Sham (KS) spectra of a DFT calculation do not provide a reliable description of the actual many-body spectra. With regard to the former, it turns out that an essential ingredient for capturing the strong electronic correlations leading to the opening of the Mott gap within DFT [23] is the notorious derivative discontinuity of exact DFT [24], which is lacking in the standard approximations like LDA and GGA. On the other hand, even if we had the exact functional or a proper approximation featuring a derivative discontinuity, the KS system as an effective one-body system cannot properly reproduce the many-body spectrum of a Mott insulator, since it must be metallic by construction. In actual fact, the exact band gap of a system is really the sum of the KS band gap and the derivative discontiuity. Thus, for a Mott insulator the band gap is entirely due to the derivative discontinuity, which offers an alternative definition of a Mott insulator.

To date most efforts to describe strongly correlated materials on an ab initio basis concentrate on combining DFT calculations with DMFT calculations for a strongly correlated subset of orbitals [25, 26, 27]. While this DFT+DMFT approach has been quite successful, the notorious double-counting problem inherent to this type of approaches remains essentially unsolved [28]. Combining a Green’s function based ab initio method such as the GW approximation with DMFT solves this problem, but comes at a considerable computational cost [29, 30].

Recently, substantial progress has been made in the application of DFT to strongly correlated problems. First, it has been shown that DFT can capture certain aspects of the Kondo effect in the Anderson impurity model, provided that the exchange-correlation (xc) potential has steps at integer values of the impurity occupation, related to the derivative discontinuity [31, 32, 33]. Second, we have shown that the actual many-body spectral function can be extracted from a ground state DFT calculation, by making use of steady-state DFT (or i-DFT for brief) in a specific limit, called the ideal STM limit, where the KS equations for the density and the current decouple and the density becomes the equilibrium one [34]. This approach has been successfully applied to the Anderson impurity model, where it correctly captures the spectral function, both inside and outside the Kondo regime. Moreover, the approach can also be applied to calculate spectra of bulk systems, for example, to the Hubbard model, where it correctly describes the metal-insulator transition in the spectral function [35].

The central ingredient for computing the spectra in the i-DFT framework is the xc bias, i.e., the xc contribution to the applied bias voltage, which is a functional of the density and the current. In order to correctly capture both the Kondo peak in the Anderson impurity model, as well as the quasiparticle peak in the metallic phase of the Hubbard model, the electron density and spectral function need to comply with Fermi-liquid theory [36, 37, 38]. In our previous work we exploited this connection to derive exact conditions on the xc bias from Fermi-liquid theory for describing the Mott transition in the Hubbard model at particle-hole symmetry [35].

Here, we are going to generalize and extend the Fermi-liquid conditions on the xc bias to obtain local spectral functions in the absence of particle-hole symmetry. Importantly, we show a simpler and more transparent way of deriving these conditions than in our previous work [35], thus establishing a clear connection between Fermi-liquid theory and i-DFT. While these conditions are rather general and could be useful for other models as well, we here apply them to construct an exchange-correlation bias for the Hubbard model away from half-filling, which in turn is applied to calculate spectral functions in the doped Mott phase. Our results show that this approach correctly describes the doping-induced Mott transition in the spectral function of the single-band Hubbard model.

2.2 Treating the model with ground state DFT: construction of an xc potential

In a first step before aiming for the spectral function, we want to treat the system of interacting electrons on the Bethe lattice with infinite coordination described by the Hamiltonion (1) within DFT. Since we are interested in the uniform system, i.e., the lattice potential vv is the same for all sites of the lattice, by symmetry the density nn on a lattice site also must be the same on all sites. The main idea of DFT is to reproduce the interacting density as the density of a fictitious, non-interacting system of electrons, the Kohn-Sham (KS) system, subject to an effective single-particle KS potential. For the uniform case, by symmetry the KS potential vsv_{s} is the same for all lattice sites and may be written as

where vHxcv_{\rm Hxc} is the Hartree-exchange-correlation (Hxc) potential which depends on the density. 3 Density functional approach to doping-driven Mott transition

3.1 Synopsis of steady-state density functional theory

Steady-state density functional theory, also called i-DFT [44], is a generalization of standard ground-state (or equilibrium) DFT to describe steady-state electronic transport through an arbitrary spatial region connected to two biased leads. It is based on a one-to-one correspondence between the local potential in the arbitrary region plus the bias across it and the corresponding (non-equilibrium) density in the region plus the steady-state current across it. The corresponding KS system then gives both the density and the steady current II, where not only the KS potential carries an Hxc contribution, but also the KS bias VsV_{s} is the sum of the external bias VV plus an xc contribution to the bias VxcV_{\rm xc}, i.e., Vs=V+VxcV_{s}=V+V_{\rm xc}. Both the Hxc contribution to the external potential as well as the xc bias are functionals of both density and current. In general, the KS equations for these two basic variables are coupled and have to be solved together self-consistently.

In the following, we will use a very particular limit of i-DFT (or any theory of electronic transport) which in Ref. [34] was called the “ideal STM limit” because it resembles the way a scanning tunneling microscope (STM) works. Assume that the following conditions are met: (i) one of the leads (which is kept at zero temperature) is coupled infinitesimally weakly to the interacting region of interest and (ii) the whole applied bias drops at this lead. Then the differential conductance for a given bias V=!V=\omega is related to the zero-temperature equilibrium spectral function of the region connected to the second lead, i.e.,

∂I∂V|V=!→�T→01�​Tr​[�𝐓​𝐀​(!)]\frac{\partial I}{\partial V}\bigg|_{V=\omega}\xrightarrow[{\mathbf{\Gamma}_{T}}\to 0]{}\frac{1}{\pi}{\rm Tr}[{\mathbf{\Gamma_{T}A}}(\omega)] (16)

where �T=i⁡(�T†−�T){\mathbf{\Gamma}_{T}}=i({\mathbf{\Sigma}_{T}}^{\dagger}-{\mathbf{\Sigma}_{T}}) with �T{\mathbf{\Sigma}_{T}} being the embedding self energy of the tip and 𝐀⁡(!){\mathbf{A}}(\omega) is the equilibrium many-body spectral function matrix.

In i-DFT, the ideal STM limit leads to a complete decoupling of the self-consistent equation for the density and the one for the current [34]. This means that one can first solve the KS for the equilibrium density and then, for this density, solve the equation for the current. This latter equation reads

I=1�​∫d​!​(fT=0​(!−Vs)−fT​(!))​Tr​[�T​𝐀s​(!)]I=\frac{1}{\pi}\int{\rm d}\omega\;(f_{T=0}(\omega-V_{s})-f_{T}(\omega))\;{\rm Tr}[\mathbf{\Gamma}_{T}\mathbf{A}_{s}(\omega)] (17)

where 𝐀s​(!){\mathbf{A}}_{s}(\omega) is the KS spectral function matrix. The coupling to the “STM tip”, i.e., the weakly coupled electrode, can be chosen at will. As we are interested in the local spectral function of our model, we choose the coupling matrix �T\mathbf{\Gamma}_{T} such that the tip only couples to the single site jj (for our model all sites are equivalent) such that (�T)j​k=�j​kT(\mathbf{\Gamma}_{T})_{jk}={}_{T}\delta_{jk} and we take T to be independent of frequency, i.e., we use the wide-band limit for the tip. As a final ingredient we realize that the above procedure can also be applied to an infinitely extended bulk system connected only to the STM tip [35]. In this case, the bulk takes on the role of the second electrode.

Putting everything together and performing the derivative of Eq. (17) with respect to the bias, in Ref. [34] we arrived at the following compact relation which expresses the (local) many-body spectral function completely in terms of KS quantities as

A⁡(!)=As​(!+Vxc)1−∂Vxc∂I~|n,I~​(!)​As​(!+Vxc)A(\omega)=\frac{A_{s}(\omega+V_{\rm xc})}{1-\left.\frac{\partial V_{\rm xc}}{\partial\tilde{I}}\right|_{n,\tilde{I}(\omega)}A_{s}(\omega+V_{\rm xc})} (18)

In Eq. (18) both the xc bias and its derivative have to be evaluated at the self-consistent current corresponding to the external bias V=!V=\omega. Realizing that the KS spectral function depends on the density n⁡(𝒓)n(\bm{r}) via the KS potential vs​(𝒓)v_{s}(\bm{r}), we see that Eq. (18) actually presents a functional relationship between the ground state density n⁡(𝒓)n(\bm{r}) and the spectral function via the xc bias. Note that the current I=I⁡(!)I=I(\omega) is merely an auxiliary quantity for determining the spectral function. Thus Eq. (18) expresses the fact that in DFT the exact spectral function is a functional of the ground state density, and defines that functional in terms of the xc bias.

Of course, in order to apply the scheme described here to the calculation of many-body spectral functions one needs an approximation for the xc bias VxcV_{\rm xc}. In the following, we first derive relations for this quantity from Fermi liquid theory. Using these relations we then construct an approximation for VxcV_{\rm xc} for the model under study. which will be exploited below a couple of times in the derivation of the Fermi liquid conditions for the xc bias.

3.2 Fermi liquid conditions for the exchange-correlation bias

We now make use of Fermi liquid theory [37, 38] and the local GF (3) in order to derive some exact conditions for the exchange-correlation bias. First, we derive relationships between the exact spectral function A⁡(!)A(\omega) and the KS spectral function As​(!)A_{s}(\omega) as well as their derivatives.

Expanding the local self-energy to first order (purely real)

3.3 Parametrization of the exchange-correlation bias for arbitrary doping

We now exploit the FL conditions (48-51) to construct an approximation for the xc bias of the Hubbard model (1) on the Bethe lattice with infinite coordination. Extensions to other lattices such as, e.g., the single cubic lattice, are expected to follow similar construction principles but obviously will require different parametrizations for, e.g., the Hxc potential or the quasiparticle weight.

Our starting point is the following ansatz for the xc bias in the Mott insulating phase in terms of the Hxc potential:

V¯xc​(n,I~)=vHxc​(n)−vHxc​(n+I~/2​�).\bar{V}_{\rm xc}(n,\tilde{I})=v_{\rm Hxc}(n)-v_{\rm Hxc}(n+\tilde{I}/2\pi)\;. (52)

This ansatz is motivated by previous experience both with the Anderson impurity model [44, 42, 34], multiple quantum dots [45], and with reverse-engineering of the xc bias in the Mott phase of the Bethe lattice from dynamical mean field theory in the non-crossing approximation similar to what has been done in the Supplemental Material of Ref. [35]. By construction (52) fulfills FL-1, V¯xc​(n,0)=0\bar{V}_{\rm xc}(n,0)=0. Panel a) of Fig. 2 shows the Mott xc bias for different values of nn for U=8(>Uc)U=8(>U_{c}). The most prominent feature of V¯xc​(n,I~)\bar{V}_{\rm xc}(n,\tilde{I}) is the sharp step of height �xc\Delta_{\rm xc} at Istp/ =2​(1−n)I^{\rm stp}/\gamma=2\,(1-n). This step is responsible for opening the gap in the insulating Mott phase [35]. We also note that V¯xc​(n,I~)\bar{V}_{\rm xc}(n,\tilde{I}) is monotonously decreasing with I~\tilde{I} which guarantees that the corresponding many-body spectral function A⁡(!)A(\omega) according to Eq. (18) is non-negative. Furthermore, due to particle-hole symmetry of the Hxc potential, vHxc​(2−n)=U−vHxc​(n)v_{\rm Hxc}(2-n)=U-v_{\rm Hxc}(n), we have that V¯xc​(2−n,−I~)=−V¯xc​(n,I~)\bar{V}_{\rm xc}(2-n,-\tilde{I})=-\bar{V}_{\rm xc}(n,\tilde{I})

Obviously, the second FL condition (49) is not fulfilled for the Mott xc bias (52), since d​V¯xc/d​I~​(0)≠0d\bar{V}_{\rm xc}/d\tilde{I}(0)\neq 0 for any nn. In order to impose FL conditions (49-51) on the xc bias, we follow our previous works and introduce a "Kondo prefactor":

Vxc​(n,I~)=aK​(I~)​V¯xc​(n,I~)V_{\rm xc}(n,\tilde{I})=a_{\rm K}(\tilde{I})\,\bar{V}_{\rm xc}(n,\tilde{I}) (53)

In order to comply with FL-2, the Kondo prefactor must vanish for the zero current, aK​(0)=0a_{\rm K}(0)=0, since

0=FL2Vxc′​(n,I~=0)=aK′​(0)​V¯xc​(n,0)⏟=0+aK​(0)​V¯xc′​(n,0)=aK​(0)​V¯xc′​(n,0)0\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm FL2}}{{=}}V_{\rm xc}^{\prime}(n,\tilde{I}=0)=a_{\rm K}^{\prime}(0)\,\underbrace{\bar{V}_{\rm xc}(n,0)}_{=0}+a_{\rm K}(0)\,\bar{V}_{\rm xc}^{\prime}(n,0)=a_{\rm K}(0)\,\bar{V}_{\rm xc}^{\prime}(n,0) (54)

where the prime denotes derivative with respect to current, i.e., Vxc′​(n,I~)=∂I~Vxc​(n,I~)V_{\rm xc}^{\prime}(n,\tilde{I})=\partial_{\tilde{I}}V_{\rm xc}(n,\tilde{I}) and aK′​(I~)=∂I~aK​(I~)a_{\rm K}^{\prime}(\tilde{I})=\partial_{\tilde{I}}a_{\rm K}(\tilde{I}). In the last step we have used that V¯xc\bar{V}_{\rm xc} complies with FL1.

On the other hand, for sufficiently large |I~||\tilde{I}| the xc bias should recover the form of the Mott xc bias, in order to reproduce the lower and upper Hubbard bands, and hence aK→1a_{\rm K}\to 1. This is achieved by choosing the following form for the prefactor:

aK​(I~)=a⁡(Y⁡(I~))​ with ​Y​(I~)=�1​I~+�2​I~2+�3​I~3+…a_{\rm K}(\tilde{I})=a(Y(\tilde{I}))\;\mbox{ with }\;Y(\tilde{I})=\lambda_{1}\tilde{I}+\lambda_{2}\tilde{I}^{2}+\lambda_{3}\tilde{I}^{3}+\ldots (55)

where the envelope function a⁡(Y)a(Y) is an odd and bounded function, with a⁡(Y)→±1a(Y)\to\pm 1 for Y→±∞Y\to\pm\infty. The specific form of aKa_{\rm K} used in the present work will be given later.

For the inner function Y⁡(I~)Y(\tilde{I}) we have chosen a polynomial of finite order nn, but without a constant term (so that Y→0Y\to 0 for I~→0\tilde{I}\to 0). We fix the coefficients �i\lambda_{i} of the polynomial via the Fermi liquid conditions, thereby enforcing them on the xc bias Vxc​(n,I~)V_{\rm xc}(n,\tilde{I}). Since conditions FL-1 and FL-2 are already enforced by the form of the xc bias given by (52) and (53), we have only two conditions left, FL-3 and FL-4, to fix the coefficients. Hence the polynomial must be quadratic, Y⁡(I~)=�1​I~+�2​I~2Y(\tilde{I})=\lambda_{1}\tilde{I}+\lambda_{2}\tilde{I}^{2}. For higher order polynomials we need additional conditions (Fermi liquid or other) to fix the addional coefficients.

Finally, we are going to exploit FL4 to fix �2\lambda_{2}. Application of FL4 to the xc bias (53) yields:

where in the last step we have used that a⁡(Y)a(Y) is an odd function, and thus a′′​(0)=0a^{\prime\prime}(0)=0.

Plugging this and the result for the first derivative (57) into (59), and solving for �2\lambda_{2}, we obtain:

�2=Z−2−16​a′​(0)​V¯xc′​(0)​As​(0)4​(As′′​(0)−3​(As′​(0))2As​(0))−V¯xc′′​(0)2​V¯xc′​(0)​�1.\lambda_{2}=\frac{Z^{-2}-1}{6\,a^{\prime}(0)\,\bar{V}_{\rm xc}^{\prime}(0)\,A_{s}(0)^{4}}\left(A_{s}^{\prime\prime}(0)-\frac{3\,(A_{s}^{\prime}(0))^{2}}{A_{s}(0)}\right)-\frac{\bar{V}_{\rm xc}^{\prime\prime}(0)}{2\,\bar{V}_{\rm xc}^{\prime}(0)}\,\lambda_{1}\,. So far we haven’t specified the specific form of the Kondo prefactor aKa_{\rm K} of Eq. (53). In previous works [34, 35] we have chosen the form

aK,1​(I~)=2�​arctan⁡(Y⁡(I~))a_{\rm K,1}(\tilde{I})=\tfrac{2}{\pi}\arctan(Y(\tilde{I})) (62)

for which also here we will present some results. However, for reasons to be explained below we will also use the form

aK,2​(I~)=tanh⁡(Y⁡(I~)).a_{\rm K,2}(\tilde{I})=\tanh(Y(\tilde{I}))\;. (63)

With these choices for the Kondo prefactors we have specified the form of our approximation to VxcV_{\rm xc}. However, another ingredient which needs to be specified is the quasiparticle weight ZZ which enters in the definintions of the parameters �1\lambda_{1} and �2\lambda_{2} of Eqs.(58) and (61), respectively. Before going to describe a parametrization for the quasiparticle weight ZZ we would also like to highlight how our functional (which uses input from Fermi liquid theory) transitions to the Mott insulating regime which cannot be described in this framework: in the Mott regime, ZZ vanishes (see below) and therefore the coefficient �2\lambda_{2} of Eq. (61) diverges (to OPEN+∞)+\infty)). Then both Kondo prefactors (62) and (63) become unity and our xc bias functional reduces to V¯xc\bar{V}_{\rm xc} which correctly describes the Mott phase.

The quasiparticle weight of our model has been computed as function of the density with NRG in Ref. [8] and we now construct a parametrization of these results. We start at the particle-hole symmetric point (n=1n=1) for which the quasiparticle weight can be parametrized as

Zph=(1+2zUc2)​[2zz2+U2−2zz2+Uc2]Z_{\rm ph}=\left(1+\frac{{}_{z}^{2}}{U_{c}^{2}}\right)\left[\frac{{}_{z}^{2}}{{}_{z}^{2}+U^{2}}-\frac{{}_{z}^{2}}{{}_{z}^{2}+U_{c}^{2}}\right] (64)

with z=4{}_{z}=4. Then for U≤UcU\leq U_{c} we parametrize the density dependence of ZZ for arbitrary density as

Z=Zph2+(1−Zph2)​(arctan⁡(b⁡(n−1))arctan⁡(b))2Z=\sqrt{Z_{\rm ph}^{2}+\left(1-Z_{\rm ph}^{2}\right)\left(\frac{\arctan(b(n-1))}{\arctan(b)}\right)^{2}} (65)

with

b=1.79−0.000469​U4.b=1.79-0.000469U^{4}\;. (66)

For U>UcU>U_{c} we still use the parametrization of Eq. (65) but with Zph=0Z_{\rm ph}=0 and the slightly different parametrization for bb

b=1.31+(U−Uc)2.b=\frac{1.3}{1+(U-U_{c})^{2}}\;. (67)

In panel b) of Fig. 2 we confirm that our parametrization of ZZ reproduces the NRG results of Ref. [8] reasonably well. With this, in principle we have all the necessary ingredients to construct an approximate xc bias which includes the Fermi-liquid conditions derived above. In panel c) we show our approximate VxcV_{\rm xc} according to the ansatz (53) for the two forms of the Kondo prefactor (62) and (63) with the coefficients �1\lambda_{1} and �2\lambda_{2} chosen according to Eqs. (58) and (61). Here we choose the densities below n=1n=1. For currents smaller than the one corresponding to the step in VxcV_{\rm xc}, our approximation is somewhat similar to the Mott xc bias V¯xc\bar{V}_{\rm xc} of Eq.(52) (shown for the same parameters in panel a) of the same figure) with one crucial difference between VxcV_{\rm xc} and V¯xc\bar{V}_{\rm xc}: around I/ ≈0I/\gamma\approx 0 by construction the xc bias VxcV_{\rm xc} becomes flat in order to satisfy the FL conditions. However, looking at the step height of VxcV_{\rm xc} of panel c) we find that it is reduced compared to the step in V¯xc\bar{V}_{\rm xc}. This latter step is given by the derivative discontinuity �xc\Delta_{\rm xc} and has the clear physical meaning of the Mott gap, a fundamental physical quantity of the system which should not be modified by the doping. We can also understand why our ansatz for VxcV_{\rm xc} leads to the reduction in the step height: the Kondo prefactor (which multiplies V¯xc\bar{V}_{\rm xc} in our ansatz) is just not yet close to unity when the current is close to the value where the step appears at Istp/ =2​(1−n)I^{\rm stp}/\gamma=2(1-n). Since by construction the Kondo prefactor is required to act close to zero current, this suggests to correct it (for U>UcU>U_{c}) in the following way (j∈{1,2}j\in\{1,2\}):

aK,jcorr.=�⁡(Istp−I)​aK,j+�⁡(I−Istp)​ for n<1a_{\rm K,j}^{\rm corr.}=\Theta(I^{\rm stp}-I)\,a_{\rm K,j}+\Theta(I-I^{\rm stp})\hbox{\hskip 28.45274pt for $n<1$} (68)

and

aK,jcorr.=�⁡(I−Istp)​aK,j+�⁡(Istp−I)​ for n>1a_{\rm K,j}^{\rm corr.}=\Theta(I-I^{\rm stp})\,a_{\rm K,j}+\Theta(I^{\rm stp}-I)\hbox{\hskip 28.45274pt for $n>1$} (69)

where �⁡(x)\Theta(x) is the Heaviside step function.

In panel d) of Fig. 2 we show the xc bias obtained with these corrected prefactors. As desired, the height of the step is now restored to its original value while preserving the FL conditions around zero current. For n<1n<1 (n>1n>1) and I>IstpI>I^{\rm stp} (I<IstpI<I^{\rm stp}) the new VxcV_{\rm xc} is now identical to the Mott xc bias V¯xc\bar{V}_{\rm xc}. Since for both versions of the Kondo prefactor, the corresponding xc biases satisfy the FL conditions, around zero current they are indistinguishable. At closer inspection away from zero current (not shown) one notes that the xc bias using aK,2a_{\rm K,2} approaches V¯xc\bar{V}_{\rm xc} faster than the one with aK,1a_{\rm K,1} which is simply due to the former approaching unity faster than the latter for large arguments.

4 Numerical results

In this Section we show results for the spectral function obtained with i-DFT using the approximations for the xc bias discussed in the previous Section. In Fig. 3 we show i-DFT spectra for U=8U=8 which leads to a derivative discontinuity of �xc≈3.42\Delta_{\rm xc}\approx 3.42. For the onsite potential we choose v=−1.87v=-1.87 which leads to a doping of �=1−n≈0.02\delta=1-n\approx 0.02. In the upper panel of this figure we show spectra obtained with the uncorrected Kondo prefactors aK,ja_{\rm K,j}, j∈{1,2}j\in\{1,2\} (Eqs. (62) and (63)) while the lower panel shows the spectra obtained with the corrected Kondo prefactors of Eq. (68). In the lower panel we also show the NRG spectrum of Ref. [6] for comparison. The inset in the lower panel zooms in around the Kondo resonance.

We see that for the lower Hubbard band the different Kondo prefactors give similar results. First of all, the appearance of the Kondo resonance is captured due to the incorporation of the FL conditions in the xc bias. The dip in the spectra just to the left of the Kondo resonance is more pronounced for aK,2a_{\rm K,2} (both the uncorrected and corrected versions) as compared to aK,1a_{\rm K,1} and thus more in line with the NRG results while the width of the Kondo resonance is reasonably well reproduced in i-DFT with both prefactors (see inset in lower panel). The big difference between the i-DFT spectra obtained with uncorrected and corrected Kondo prefactors is in the size of the Mott-Hubbard gap as well as in the shape of the upper Hubbard band. For the uncorrected Kondo prefactors the Mott-Hubbard gap (which should be given by �xc\Delta_{\rm xc}) is severely underestimated, a deficiency which is cured using the corrected prefactors, as intended. Also the upper Hubbard band coincides for the two corrected prefactors since its shape in both cases is determined solely by the Mott xc bias V¯xc\bar{V}_{\rm xc}.

In Fig. 4 more i-DFT spectral functions are shown. In panel a) we compare spectral functions for U=14U=14 with NRG results from Ref. [46] with the same overall agreement as for the case of U=8U=8, see discussion of the lower panel of Fig. 3. In panels b) to d) only the prefactor aK,2corr.a_{\rm K,2}^{\rm corr.} is used. Panel b) shows the evolution of the i-DFT spectra for U=8U=8 when changing the onsite energy. Of course, for half-filling (doping �=0\delta=0) there is no Kondo resonance which only appears at finite doping. As expected, with increased doping the resonance broadens. Panels c) and d) show spectra for different values of UU where here the onsite energies vv have been chosen such that the doping �=1−n=0.03\delta=1-n=0.03 remains constant. Obviously, the upper Hubbard bands are pushed to higher energies as UU increases because the Mott gap (i.e., �xc\Delta_{\rm xc}) increases from approximately 0.5 for U=6U=6 to 7.7 for U=12U=12. At the same time, the quantity U−�xcU-\Delta_{\rm xc} appears to converge for increasing UU: while for U=6U=6 we have U−�xc≈0.5U-\Delta_{\rm xc}\approx 0.5 for U=6U=6, 88, and 1010 the corresponding values for U−�xcU-\Delta_{\rm xc} are 4.6, 4.4, and 4.3, respectively. The quantity U−�xcU-\Delta_{\rm xc} also controls the bandwidth of the lower and upper Hubbard band. Interestingly, for fixed doping the width of the Kondo peak in our i-DFT approach also appears to converge as UU increases, see panel d). This is probably not a coincidence. For fixed and small doping the KS potential should be small and the quasiparticle weight changes essentially linearly with doping and becomes independent of UU. Then the only ingredient in VxcV_{\rm xc} which depends on the interaction is the Mott xc bias V¯xc\bar{V}_{\rm xc} of Eq. (52). Assuming that the function g⁡(x)g(x) of Eq. (13) is only weakly dependent on UU, the remaining dependence of vHxcv_{\rm Hxc} (Eq. (12)) and thus V¯xc\bar{V}_{\rm xc} on the interaction is only through the factor U−�xcU-\Delta_{\rm xc}.

Fig. 5 shows 3D plots of the spectral function as a function of !\omega and applied gate vv for two different values of UU. The left panel shows the spectral function for U=5.8U=5.8, just in the metallic regime at particle-hole symmetry. At the paticle-hole symmetric point (v=−U/2=−2.9v=-U/2=-2.9) we thus see the sharp quasiparticle peak at !=0\omega=0, together with the two Hubbard side bands symmetrically placed at !=±U/2=±2.9\omega=\pm U/2=\pm 2.9. As vv is increased, the quasiparticle peak becomes broader, gaining weight and eventually merging with the lower Hubbard band as the density approaches zero, n→0n\to 0. On the other hand, the upper Hubbard band, continuously decreases both in weigth and width, eventually disappearing completely as n→0n\to 0.

The right panel shows the spectral function for U=8U=8, deep in the Mott phase. Thus at the particle-hole symmetric point v=−U/2=−4v=-U/2=-4, there is no quasiparticle peak, the spectrum is gapped. As vv increases, at first the only effect is the shifting of both Hubbard bands with the applied gate. But when the critical gate for the doping-driven Mott transition, vc=U2​(�c​(U)−1)∼−2.29v_{c}=\tfrac{U}{2}(\eta_{c}(U)-1)\sim-2.29, is reached, a sharp quasiparticle appears at !=0\omega=0. Again, as vv increase the quasiparticle peak becomes broder and gains weight, eventually merging with the lower Hubbard band, while width and weight of the upper Hubbard decrease, eventually disappearing completely as n→0n\to 0.

Fig. 5 also shows some limitations of our approximation to the xc bias functional. In the limit of low occupation, n→0n\to 0, the spectral function does not converge to the non-interacting (i.e. the KS) spectral function given by Eq. (5). Most likely, this is due to our parametrization of the quasiparticle weight not approaching unity fast enough in the limit n→0n\to 0. Hence Z−2−1Z^{-2}-1 in the numerator of Eq. (61) does not vanish fast enough in the limit n→0n\to 0 to compensate both for As​(0)4A_{s}(0)^{4} in the denominator going to zero extremely fast as well as for the divergence of As′​(0)A_{s}^{\prime}(0) in the same limit. This prevents �2\lambda_{2} from vanishing in this limit, as it should. We suspect that the problem can be fixed by a more careful parametrization of ZZ in this limit.

5 Conclusion

In the present work we have shown how one can capture the doping-driven Mott transition within the framework of steady-state density functional theory (i-DFT). By construction, standard DFT in principle gives access to the many-body density of an interacting many-electron system but requires (an approximation of) the Hxc potential as functional of the equilibrium density. A central but rarely used tenet of standard DFT is that since the external potential of the many-electron system is a functional of the density, in principle all eigenstates of the many-body Hamiltonian (and properties derived from these eigenstates) are functionals of the density. Of course, typcially the functional form of these functionals is unknown.

In the so-called “ideal STM limit”, i-DFT gives access to equilibrium many-body spectral functions provided (an approximation of) the xc contribution to the bias is known as functional of both density and current. Since in this limit, the i-DFT equations for density and current are completely decoupled, conceptually one may view the i-DFT access to spectral functions as a particular way to write the many-body spectral function as a functional of the equilibrium density, an explicit form of which is given by Eq. (18).

In the present work we have constructed an approximate functional for the xc bias for interacting electrons on the Bethe lattice with infinite coordination. This model plays a central role in DMFT and may be viewed as one of the minimal models to study the Mott metal-insulator transition. In order to construct an approximate xc bias, we first established a connection between the (many-body) quasiparticle weight and the xc bias to lowest orders in the current by employing an expression for the Green function of Fermi Liquid theory around zero frequency. We used these analytical FL conditions to fix two parameters in our ansatz for the xc bias. Due to this construction one can expect the i-DFT spectra to reproduce the slope and second derivative of many-body spectra around zero frequency, i.e., the location of the quasiparticle resonance (if present). Other important ingredients of our functional are (i) the famous xc contribution to the derivative discontinuity of DFT which we could, for our model system, connect to the plateau of the density as function of onsite energies studied with DMFT+NRG in Ref. [7] and (ii) the quasiparticle weight as function of the density obtained with NRG [8] for which we found a simple parametrization.

The i-DFT spectra computed with our approximation for the xc bias reproduce the main features of reference spectra of systems with small doping such as the Kondo resonance and the Hubbard sidebands reasonably well. One feature which our functional does not capture very well is the pronounced dip between the Kondo resonance and the lower (upper) Hubbard band for densities n<1n<1 (n>1n>1). We have tried two forms of the prefactor multiplying the Mott part of the xc bias in our ansatz. Compared to the first Kondo prefactor, the second one which approaches unity faster for larger arguments leads to somewhat stronger dips than the first one. However, even for this prefactor the dips are still not as pronounced as in the NRG results.

In general, our i-DFT approach for the calculation of many-body spectral functions is computationally extremely efficient. It requires the solution of (i) a standard KS equation to obtain the self-consistent density of the system and (ii) for each frequency, i.e., bias, the self-consistent solution of another self-consistent equation for the current. This computational efficiency allows for rapid multi-parameter scans as, e.g., scans of both onsite energies and frequencies.

Another important result of the present work is the establishment of a theoretical connection between the quasiparticle weight, a quantity well-known from many-body Green function theory and the xc bias, which is the quintessential i-DFT quantity which needs to be approximated in practice. We expect this connection to be useful for applications of i-DFT to model systems beyond the one studied here.

Our work also points the way for future research towards an ab initio description of Mott insulators and strongly correlated materials in general. For instance, one could envision mapping the standard DFT electronic structure of a correlated material onto a few level model which then can be treated with i-DFT. Possible difficulties along the way could be the proper extraction of model parameters that avoid the notorious double-counting problem of DFT++ approaches [28], perhaps by making use of a different type of mapping between lattice DFT and real-space DFT [47]. A further challenge could be the construction of a reasonable approximation of the quasiparticle weight as a functional of the density.
